title: Pocket Wisdom
excerpt: I carried a small card in my wallet for years. One sentence from it still runs through my head in almost every conversation I have.
body:
I carried a small card in my wallet for years. One sentence from it still runs through my head in almost every conversation I have.

People often told me how fortunate I was to start my professional career at Datatel (which merged with SunGard Higher Education in 2012 to become Ellucian), but I didn’t appreciate that until I’d lived long enough to have something to compare it to. Now I can truly see how lucky I was to land there. I see Datatel’s reflection in so many leaders. Often, when I coach a former Datatel colleague and marvel at their leadership foundation, I find myself thinking about how Datatel invested in its leaders and employees, and how those investments paid off in ways that are hard to measure.

I draw on so many pearls of wisdom from my early days at Datatel, but I still share one in particular with clients, colleagues, and friends.

Datatel Basics

When I started at Datatel, I was given a tri-fold card that fit in my wallet. It had our Vision & Philosophy on the front, and inside were twenty Datatel Basics. These were single sentences that listed the fundamentals every employee should follow to embody our company culture. I remember having one of the basics listed on each pay stub. Datatel did something right, at least for me, because those basics sank in and shaped my early professional identity.

Unfortunately, I no longer have any versions of my Datatel Basics cards. All I have is an old photo of the front of one. If a colleague reading this still has one, please post pictures. I imagine DeAnn Jelinek, our company historian, still has all the versions.

I still remember two word for word. The first one gives you a sense of how far back this goes. Datatel Basic #7, “Check your voice mail at least twice a day and E-mail at least every other day.”

You read that right. In my early days, e-mail was novel enough that we were only expected to check it every other day. Apparently it was also worthy of capitalization. This brings back fond memories of changing my voicemail greeting each morning. “You’ve reached Josh Dietrich at Datatel. Today is November 16th, and I’m in the office; however, I will be in meetings for most of the day.” I took pride in demonstrating to whoever was calling that I had the rigor to update my voicemail greeting daily.

The other basic that sticks with me is more substantial. Looking back, I can see how this basic has shaped my interactions with everyone around me.

“Always act to increase the client’s confidence in Datatel.”

That sounds simple enough. If you truly take this to heart, you’ll find this simple statement teaches lesson after lesson over time. I realize that this mantra lives rent-free in my head in nearly every interaction. “Am I acting in a manner that increases this person’s confidence in me? My company or the organization I’m representing?” The basic focuses on clients, but the same is true when interacting with your employees, your friends, even your family.

Increasing Confidence

Often this wisdom arrives in hindsight. We have an interaction with someone, client or otherwise, and it doesn’t go as well as we’d like. On reflection, we find we said or did something that didn't increase their confidence. Each time we do this, we strengthen our awareness muscles, which improves how we show up the next time. I’ve come across countless examples that have served as learning moments.

The development team gets a customer support ticket escalated to them. After reviewing the ticket, they meet with the client and attempt to show empathy. “Wow, I’m really sorry it took this long to get this escalated. Our support team does this all the time. They really should have passed this to development a month ago.” This attempt at empathy may build the client’s confidence in the development team, but it undermines their confidence in support, and likely the company as a whole.

Or we tell a client we’ll get back to them by Friday. Friday comes and goes, and we don’t close the loop. No one complains, but their confidence slips a little.

Or the overly transparent, “Honestly, we’ve never tested our product at your scale.” Sometimes that level of transparency is necessary and appropriate. Other times, it just erodes confidence.

Sometimes this is about what you say, but often it’s about how you act. Actions speak louder than words, as we are fond of saying. Changing my voicemail greeting each morning was a simple act. When someone called and reached my voicemail, hearing that I’d been in earlier that day to update my greeting gave them confidence I’d be back the next day, and it was reasonable to assume I’d get their message within 24 hours. On the other hand, if my greeting says it’s November 1st, and it’s actually November 16th, they are likely to assume I’m unreliable. In case you’re wondering, no, I no longer change my voicemail greeting. I’m not even sure what my greeting says anymore.

Why It Works

I could go on. I think I’ve shared this wisdom at least a dozen times this year alone. What I find interesting is I never took the time to think about why this Datatel Basic had such a positive effect on me. I can see it clearly now. It all comes back to awareness.

If you take this basic to heart, it stays in your awareness and rises every time you find yourself choosing what to say or do. Often, when we say something we regret, we realize in hindsight that we spoke on autopilot. We act without thinking.

This simple statement invites you to pause and, most importantly, to take the client’s perspective. Rather than viewing the impact of this action through my own eyes, or even through my company's, let me shift my perspective to my client's. If I choose this action, how will that land with my client? Will this increase their confidence in me? Or will it decrease their confidence?

A seasoned professional services consultant does this intuitively. They have thousands of reps of saying or doing this and seeing the reaction on their clients' faces. A newly promoted leader, or a developer interacting directly with clients for the first time, doesn’t necessarily have that experience. But we can all learn and strengthen these muscles.

Putting It Into Practice

Think about an important relationship in your life. It could be a key client, your boss, another colleague, your partner, or a close friend. Consider how you show up with them, in your words and your actions. Are you acting in a way that builds their confidence in you?

If you’re not sure, consider asking them directly. What behaviors do I exhibit with you that build your confidence in me? What behaviors would you suggest I change to increase your confidence in me?

Tales of Wanderment

It’s my final week in Bethany Beach. This was not two months at the beach. Most days I didn’t visit the ocean. It was two months of solitude. An opportunity to go inward, after two and a half months staying with others and “feeling on” most of the time. It has been incredibly refreshing and nourishing.

The past few days, I’ve been graced with Bald Eagles at the end of my morning run. Such majestic beauty as they glide through the sky.

Last week, I saw my Fox again on the other side of town. They are on the move, perhaps reminding me it’s time for me to get moving as well.
